questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the key difference between data management and data governance?
options: Data management is the day-to-day operational work; data governance is the decisions, roles, and rules that determine how that work is supposed to happen
Data management only applies to Salesforce; data governance only applies to spreadsheets
They are the same activity under two different names
Data governance is performed only by external auditors, never by internal staff
questions.explain: Management is the operational work (entering, updating, reporting on data); governance is the upstream layer of roles, policy, and process that determines how that operational work should happen in the first place.

questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that a Salesforce org needs its own governance lens beyond a generic IT policy?
options: Generic IT policy is always wrong and should be ignored
A generic policy like "protect PII" doesn't get implemented until it's translated to a specific object, field, owner, and Salesforce feature that enforces it
Salesforce orgs are not subject to any IT policy
Governance only applies to on-premises databases, not cloud CRM platforms
questions.explain: An abstract policy only becomes real once it names the specific object/field it applies to, who's accountable, and which concrete Salesforce feature (like a Validation Rule or Platform Encryption) enforces it.

questions.q: A company configures Shield Platform Encryption on several fields (technology) but never writes down which fields should be encrypted or why (policy). Per this lesson's four-pillar model, what's the likely failure mode?
options: No failure, since technology alone is sufficient
The fields get encrypted correctly and the decision never needs revisiting
The encryption configuration becomes arbitrary and hard to justify or maintain consistently, since there's no written policy backing the technical choice
The org will be automatically non-compliant with every data privacy law
questions.explain: The lesson describes technology without policy as getting "configured arbitrarily" — the four pillars work together, and missing one (here, policy) undermines the others.

questions.q: In the three-org ungoverned-data scenario (Sales, Service, Marketing, each with its own Account object), what is identified as the root cause of the problems described — duplicate Accounts, an unclear system of record, and a failed data-deletion request?
options: Salesforce's platform architecture makes multi-org deployments technically impossible
Nobody decided who owns Account data, what counts as a duplicate, or how long records live, and then kept enforcing those decisions over time
The company didn't purchase enough Salesforce licenses
Marketing campaigns are inherently unreliable regardless of data quality
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that the platform isn't at fault — the absence of governance decisions, and the absence of ongoing enforcement of those decisions, is what produced the mess.

questions.q: Which of the four governance pillars does "a quarterly data-quality review meeting" belong to, per this lesson's definitions?
options: Technology, because it happens using a computer
People, because only people attend meetings
Process, because it's a recurring, scheduled activity that keeps policy real over time
It doesn't belong to any of the four pillars
questions.explain: Process is defined in this lesson as the recurring, scheduled activities that keep policy enforced over time — a quarterly review is exactly that kind of activity, distinct from the people (roles) or technology (tools) pillars.
